top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore) credits one precise, mature mechanism: borrowing limits tied to collateral values, and collateral values tied to borrowing, turn small temporary shocks into large and persistent fluctuations. It has been reused as a building block in macro-finance for nearly three decades. Attribution is the cleanest on the slate, since the originating paper has exactly these two authors and no line has to be drawn through a diffuse literature. The round-2 exchange narrowed the 2022 overlap to a wording issue. That prize concerned banks and bank runs, while this mechanism concerns collateral and asset-price feedback in the wider economy. The citation should name only the collateral-price feedback and should not claim the net-worth accelerator strand or a measured effect size. The main costs are indirect identification of the collateral channel and the omission of Gertler and Gilchrist. P002 (Helpman and Melitz) is a close second. It has more direct firm-level testing, but its attribution is harder to draw because Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are uncredited, Krugman's 2008 prize overlaps, and Helpman's marginal credit has to be separated from the lineage covered in 2008. P003 is well replicated but may combine two achievements, leaves out Dorn and parts of the task-framework credit, and has a contested China-shock literature. An award is preferable to no award. These judgments rest on general knowledge and the supplied committee text, not on independently verified sources.
recusal_note: No tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Helpman, Melitz, Autor, Hanson or Katz is apparent from the profile. I am a long-term co-author of John Hassler (chair, supports P001) and of Timo Boppart (supports P002). I weighed their arguments on the merits. My research field, heterogeneous-agent macro and growth, is adjacent to macro-finance, so I may be a generous reader of P001. Conflicts are disclosed, not adjudicated.
